theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the smallest number of members who must be present for a meeting to make valid decisions called?
What name is given to the official written record of a meeting?

Which agenda item, usually near the end, lets members raise minor points not listed? Give its usual name.
What is a formal proposal put to a meeting for a decision called?
What is the usual title of the person who leads a meeting and keeps order?
Eight people attend a meeting lasting 1.5 hours. How many person-hours of staff time does it use?
What three-word term describes a situation where a member's personal gain could affect a decision they help to make?
What is it called when a meeting is formally paused, to continue at a later time?
What is the person who formally supports a motion after it has been proposed called?
What is the chair's extra vote, used only to break a tie where the rules allow it, called?
What is the agenda item called in which the meeting follows up points from the last minutes?
accepted: matters arising from the last minutes

shortAnswers.stem: What is the written message that gives members the date, time and place of a meeting called?
What is a meeting called in which every member joins from a different place through an online video platform?
A meeting starts at 9:30 a.m. Its four items are timed at 15, 25, 30 and 20 minutes. At what time should it end?

essays.stem: You must plan a quarterly review meeting for 12 supervisors from branches in Kingston, May Pen and Montego Bay. Describe your plan, from setting the purpose to sending out the papers.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing the purpose with the regional manager: to review each branch's results against target and agree three actions for next quarter. From that I would decide who must attend (the 12 supervisors, the regional manager and a finance officer for the figures) and what format suits. As travel from three parishes costs time and money, I would weigh a face-to-face meeting in May Pen, which is central, against an online or hybrid meeting. Next I would fix a date with enough notice under our rules, book the venue or platform, and check access and equipment. I would draft the agenda with timed items, putting the decision items early, and ask each supervisor for a one-page branch summary in a set format. I would send the notice, agenda and papers together at least a week ahead, ask for apologies, and confirm a chair and a minute-taker.
markingPoints: Sets a clear purpose and expected outcomes first
Chooses attendees and a suitable format (face-to-face, online or hybrid), with reasons such as cost and travel
Fixes date, venue or platform and checks access and equipment, with proper notice
Builds a timed agenda with decision items placed early
Sends agenda and papers in advance, with roles (chair, minute-taker) confirmed

essays.stem: Explain how you would build the agenda for a two-hour meeting that has information items, discussion items and decision items. Justify the order and timing you choose.
essays.modelAnswer: I would list every item and label it as information, discussion or decision, with the person leading it and the papers needed. The opening items are short: welcome, apologies, approval of the last minutes and matters arising, about ten minutes in all. I would then place the decision items, because members are fresh and we must leave time for questions; each gets a time based on how complex it is, for example 25 minutes for a budget decision. Discussion items come next, with a clear question for the group so the talk has a point. Information items go last or are sent as papers to be noted, since they need little meeting time. I would add a short any other business slot and the next meeting date. I would leave about ten minutes of slack, as items often overrun. Each item shows the outcome wanted, so the chair can steer and the minute-taker knows what to record.
markingPoints: Classifies items as information, discussion or decision, with leads and papers
Places routine opening items briefly at the start
Puts decision items early while members are fresh, with justified timings
Moves information items late or to papers to save time
Builds in slack time and states the outcome wanted for each item

essays.stem: Compare face-to-face, online and hybrid meetings for a firm with staff in several parishes. Recommend when each should be used.
essays.modelAnswer: Face-to-face meetings build trust and make it easier to read body language and handle sensitive or difficult issues, such as restructuring or conflict. Their costs are travel, time away from work and venue hire. Online meetings save travel and can be called quickly, which suits short updates, regular team check-ins and members in distant parishes. Their weaknesses are poor internet links, screen fatigue and members who multitask; the chair must work harder to bring people in. Hybrid meetings let some people meet in the room while others join online, which helps when most staff are at head office but a few are away. They are the hardest to run fairly, because online members are easily left out, so they need a good camera and microphone, a chair who calls on online members by name, and shared documents on screen. I recommend face-to-face for sensitive matters and planning days, online for routine updates, and hybrid only where the equipment and chairing skills are in place.
markingPoints: Face-to-face: strengths (trust, sensitive issues) and costs (travel, time)
Online: strengths (cost, speed, reach) and weaknesses (connection, engagement)
Hybrid: benefits and the risk that online members are left out
Explains what is needed to make online or hybrid meetings work
Gives a justified recommendation of when to use each

essays.stem: Evaluate the ways a chairperson can manage a meeting in which one member dominates and another becomes hostile.
essays.modelAnswer: Prevention is the first tool: a clear agenda, agreed ground rules and time limits make it easier to step in without seeming personal. With a dominant member, the chair can thank them for their view, summarise it briefly and then invite named others to speak, or go round the table so each person has a turn. This works well because it is polite and fair, but the chair must be firm if the behaviour continues and may speak to the person privately at the break. With a hostile member, the chair should stay calm, acknowledge the concern, and bring the discussion back to the issue rather than the person. A short break can lower tension. If the hostility is about a real grievance, the chair can offer to deal with it outside the meeting. As a last resort, under the meeting's rules, the chair may ask the person to leave, but this damages relationships and should be rare. Firm, fair and early action is most effective.
markingPoints: Prevention: agenda, ground rules and time limits
Dominant member: acknowledge, summarise, invite others or go round the table
Hostile member: stay calm, acknowledge, focus on the issue not the person; use a break
Deal with personal grievances privately; removal only as a last resort under the rules
Evaluates which methods work best and why (early, firm and fair action)

essays.stem: Compare consensus, a majority vote and a decision by the chair after discussion. Recommend which a manager should use for (a) a new staff welfare policy and (b) an urgent safety problem.
essays.modelAnswer: Consensus means discussing until everyone can accept the outcome. It builds strong support and uses everyone's ideas, but it takes time and may end in a weak compromise. A majority vote is quick and clear and suits formal committees, but the losing side may feel ignored and give little support. A decision by the chair after discussion lets the person with authority decide once views are heard. It is fast and keeps accountability clear, but it can feel imposed if people think their views were not weighed. For a staff welfare policy, I recommend working towards consensus, because staff must accept and live with the policy, and there is usually time to consult. A vote can be used at the end if a few points remain. For an urgent safety problem, the manager should take advice from those present and then decide at once, because delay could put people at risk. She should explain the decision and review it later.
markingPoints: Consensus: support and ideas versus time and weak compromise
Majority vote: quick and clear versus losers feeling ignored
Chair decides after discussion: speed and accountability versus feeling imposed
Recommends consensus (or consultation) for the welfare policy, with a reason
Recommends a prompt decision by the manager for the urgent safety problem, with a reason

essays.stem: Describe how you would take, draft, check and circulate the minutes of a management meeting. Explain what makes minutes good.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting I would set up a template from the agenda, with the date, place, attendance and apologies, and a space under each item for discussion points, decisions and actions. During the meeting I would note who was present, the main points briefly, the exact wording of each decision, and each action with its owner and due date. If a decision is unclear I would ask the chair to restate it. Within two or three working days I would type the draft in the past tense and neutral language, without opinions or word-for-word speech, and send it to the chair to check. Once the chair agrees it, I would circulate it to members and action owners, marked as a draft until approved at the next meeting. Good minutes are accurate, brief and neutral; they show clearly what was decided, who does what and by when, and they protect confidential matters.
markingPoints: Prepares a template from the agenda before the meeting
Records attendance, decisions exactly, and actions with owners and dates; checks unclear decisions
Drafts promptly in neutral, past-tense language without opinions
Chair checks the draft; circulated to members and owners; approved at next meeting
States qualities of good minutes: accurate, brief, neutral, clear actions, confidentiality respected

essays.stem: Explain how a meeting manager makes sure that decisions are carried out after the meeting.
essays.modelAnswer: The work starts in the meeting: each decision should end with a named owner, a clear task and a due date, which the chair confirms before moving on. Straight after the meeting, the manager sends an action log to members and owners, even before the full minutes are ready. She keeps this log in a shared place and updates it as tasks are done. Midway to each due date she checks in with owners, asking about progress and any barriers, such as a lack of budget or a need for another department's help, and helps remove them or escalates them to someone with authority. Actions that will be late are flagged early so plans can change. At the next meeting, the action log is reviewed under matters arising, and completed items are closed. Owners who repeatedly miss dates are spoken to privately. This steady routine makes it clear that meeting decisions matter and will be followed through.
markingPoints: Each decision ends with an owner, a task and a due date confirmed in the meeting
Action log sent promptly and kept in a shared, updated place
Checks progress before due dates and helps remove barriers or escalates
Reviews actions at the next meeting and closes completed items
Deals with repeated missed actions and builds a culture of follow-through

essays.stem: Staff at your firm say that meetings waste their time. Plan how you would evaluate and improve the firm's meetings over three months.
essays.modelAnswer: In the first month I would gather evidence. I would list all regular meetings, their purpose, length, attendees and staff-time cost, and run a short anonymous survey asking whether each meeting is needed, starts on time and leads to action. I would also sit in on a sample of meetings and check how many actions from their minutes were completed. In the second month I would act on the findings. Meetings with no clear purpose would be stopped or replaced by email updates. The rest would get a timed agenda sent in advance, a shorter standard length, only the people needed for each item, and an action log. I would offer a short session for chairs on keeping to time and drawing in quiet members. In the third month I would repeat the survey and the cost count, compare the results with the starting point, and report to senior management with further recommendations. Improvements would then be built into the firm's meeting guidelines.
markingPoints: Gathers evidence first: list of meetings, costs, survey, observation, action completion
Stops or replaces meetings with no clear purpose
Sets standards: timed agendas in advance, shorter length, right attendees, action logs
Builds chairing skills
Re-measures after changes, compares with the start and reports with recommendations

essays.stem: Explain how confidential and personal information should be handled before, during and after a meeting that discusses staff matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting, papers with staff details should be marked confidential and sent only to members who are entitled to see them, through a secure route such as a password-protected file rather than a general email list. Only the personal details needed for the decision should be included. During the meeting, the chair should remind members that the item is confidential, hold it in a private room or a closed online session, and make sure no one outside can hear or see screens. The item can be taken as a closed session, with visitors asked to leave. In the minutes, the confidential item should be recorded briefly, perhaps in a separate confidential minute with limited circulation. After the meeting, printed papers should be collected or shredded, and electronic copies kept in a restricted folder. This follows the general aims of the data protection law: collect only what is needed, use it only for its purpose, keep it secure and do not keep it longer than necessary.
markingPoints: Before: mark confidential, limit circulation, secure sending, only needed details
During: remind members, private room or closed session, screens and voices protected
Minutes: brief or separate confidential minute with limited circulation
After: collect or shred papers; restricted storage for electronic copies
Links to the general aims of the data protection law (purpose, minimum data, security, retention)

essays.stem: Justify when a manager should cancel or replace a regular meeting, and say what she could use instead.
essays.modelAnswer: A regular meeting should earn its place on the calendar. A manager should cancel or replace it when there are no decisions to make, when the agenda is only updates that people could read, when key people cannot attend so nothing can be settled, or when the cost in staff time is greater than the value it adds. For example, ten supervisors meeting for an hour each week costs a great deal of time if they only report figures already in the system. Instead, she could send a short written update or dashboard each week and ask for questions by email. A 15-minute stand-up briefing can replace a long meeting for daily coordination. A shared online document or project board lets people update progress at any time. For one decision that needs two or three people, a short phone or video call is quicker. She should still keep a meeting where discussion, problem-solving or relationship-building is needed, and she should explain any change to the team so that communication does not suffer.
markingPoints: Gives sound reasons to cancel: no decisions, updates only, key people absent, cost greater than value
Uses an example or cost reasoning
Offers alternatives: written update or dashboard, short stand-up, shared online board, short call
Recognises when a meeting is still needed (discussion, problem-solving, relationships)
Explains the change to the team so communication is kept up

practical1.title: Plan, chair and minute a decision meeting
practical1.brief: Your group is the management team of a training centre. The assessor gives you a short scenario that needs a decision (for example, how to cut the electricity bill by 15% or how to arrange staff cover over the Christmas period). Plan and hold a 30-minute meeting to reach a decision. Give each member a named role: chair, meeting secretary (minute-taker), presenter of the main item, finance or facts officer, and (in a group of five) timekeeper and observer. Together, write the notice and a timed agenda, and a one-page paper for the main item with a recommendation. Hold the meeting while the assessor watches: everyone must speak on at least one item. Afterwards the secretary drafts the minutes and action log, the chair checks them, and the group completes a short evaluation of the meeting. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computer or laptop with word processor and printer, or flipchart and paper
Meeting notice, agenda, minutes and action log templates (or blank paper)
photos: The notice and timed agenda, with each member's name and role
The one-page paper for the main item, showing its recommendation
The meeting in progress, with the chair leading and the secretary taking notes
The draft minutes and action log, with owners and due dates
The completed evaluation forms and the group's summary of what to improve
checklist: Took a clear named role and carried it out (chair, secretary, presenter, facts officer, timekeeper or observer)
Helped set a clear purpose and a timed agenda with the decision item placed early
Prepared or checked their part of the meeting paper, with accurate facts and figures
Spoke clearly and respectfully, listened, and kept to the agenda and time
Helped the meeting reach and record a clear decision with actions, owners and dates
Chair: kept order, brought in every member and summed up; Secretary: produced accurate, neutral minutes
Took part in the evaluation and suggested one improvement
safety: Keep any real staff or trainee names and personal details out of the scenario and the minutes
Treat the meeting papers as confidential and collect or shred spare copies at the end
Speak respectfully: disagree with ideas, not people
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break if working at a computer for long

practical2.title: Run an online follow-up meeting and track the actions
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of poor sample papers from a past meeting: a vague agenda, minutes full of opinion and no clear actions. First, rewrite them: a clear timed agenda for a 20-minute online follow-up meeting, corrected minutes, and an action log in a spreadsheet with owners, due dates and status. Then hold the follow-up meeting on the online platform the Centre uses, with members joining from separate computers or phones in different rooms. Give each member a named role: host and chair, technical lead (sets up the link, tests sound, shares the screen), secretary, action-log keeper, and (in a group of five) a member who prepares a short cost count of the meeting in staff time. At the end, the action-log keeper updates the spreadsheet on screen and sends the action points to all members. Take screenshots and photos at each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Sample poor meeting papers from the assessor
Computers or phones with the Centre's online meeting platform and headsets
Separate rooms or quiet spaces for members
photos: The original poor papers beside the group's rewritten agenda and minutes
The meeting invitation and the platform test (screenshot)
The online meeting in progress, with a shared screen and members visible (screenshot)
The action log spreadsheet on screen, with owners, dates and status filled in
The sent message with action points to all members (screenshot)
The staff-time cost count of the meeting
checklist: Took a named role and carried it out (chair, technical lead, secretary, action-log keeper or cost counter)
Rewrote their share of the papers in clear, neutral language with timed items and clear actions
Joined the online meeting on time, with working sound, and followed online etiquette
Chair: kept to time, called on each member by name and summed up decisions
Action log: each action has one owner, a due date and a status; spreadsheet set out clearly
Cost count worked out correctly from the times and hourly rates given
Gave or received constructive feedback on how the online meeting could be improved
safety: Get everyone's agreement before any part of the meeting is recorded
Do not share passwords or meeting links outside the group
Use made-up names and figures only; no real personal data
Sit comfortably, keep the volume of headsets at a safe level, and take short screen breaks
